summary:
Legal gender recognition in Sweden was revised by two acts the Riksdag approved in April 2024, one on legal gender and one on medical procedures performed on genitalia, both in force from 1 July 2025. The Legal Gender Recognition Act simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but stops short of full self-determination; medical conditions remain part of the process, so a trans visitor updating Swedish documentation may still have to satisfy them.

The April 2024 vote was 234 to 94. From 1 July 2025 the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis fell from 18 to 16, on a doctor's or psychologist's statement plus approval from the National Board of Health and Welfare, with guardian consent required for 16 and 17 year olds. Genital surgery is restricted to those 18 and over, and gonad removal to those 23 and over unless an exceptional reason applies.

Changing-room access is not settled. In October 2025 the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their own changing rooms, a restriction that reaches ordinary public facilities rather than any specialised setting.

Transgender identity and expression were added to Swedish hate-crime legislation on 1 July 2018, and to the hate-speech provision with effect from 1 January 2019; sexual orientation had been covered in hate-crime law since 2010 and in hate speech since 1 January 2003. The National Council for Crime Prevention (Brå) published report 2024:13, a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police recorded LGBTQI hate-crime motives, which is the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

Application of the hate-speech law has been contested. Authorities declined to prosecute a Halmstad imam who described homosexuality as a virus in 2015, and the Pentecostal preacher Åke Green was convicted and then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held that European Convention protections for religious speech barred punishment.

Clinical access has narrowed. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers and gender-affirming hormones to under-16s, and to 16 to 18 year olds outside approved clinical trials. On 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare issued guidance that puberty blockers should be used only in exceptional cases and rested on uncertain evidence; this is guidance rather than a statutory ban, and misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors circulated abroad and was cited by US Republican politicians. Board data released in 2026 showed that prescriptions of puberty blockers to trans children had risen slightly since the 2022 guidance.

A bill before the Riksdag would extend protection to victims of conversion practices carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure.

Trans status was removed from the national illness classification by the National Board of Health and Welfare in January 2017, ending the diagnostic framing of trans identity in Swedish health records.

Until 2013 a legal gender change required sterilisation and sex reassignment surgery. The requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag that July; a law passed in March 2018 compensated roughly 600 to 700 people 225,000 SEK each for forced sterilisation.

On partner recognition, the Church Council of the Church of Sweden decided in November 2025, by 141 votes, that newly ordained priests must be willing to marry couples the church classes as same-sex.

Opposition to trans rights is organised. The Sweden Democrats and the Christian Democrats oppose trans legal reform while presenting it as defence of women's rights and Swedish values, and the Swedish Women's Lobby, an umbrella of 57 associations, launched the Women's Platform for Action International in 2025 to promote sex-based rights. Scholars describe the pattern as de-democratisation and record political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialised activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification.
tangentialFactors:
The 2019 Spartacus Gay Travel Index, reported by Newsweek, placed Sweden level with Canada and Portugal as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations in that edition, a third-party indicator of destination standing rather than a measure of trans-specific conditions.

An open-access study in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (February 2016) traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014, the historical record behind current service conditions.

The age of consent has been equal at 15 since 1972, and same-sex sexual activity was legalised in 1944 at an age of consent of 18. Homosexuality was declassified as an illness in October 1979. A 1987 law banning sex in gay saunas and prostitution, passed to combat HIV, was repealed in 2004.
localsOnly:
RFSL counselling centres in Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö assist people with contact to authorities and with legal assistance on matters such as asylum and wills.

In 2021 the National Board of Health and Welfare cut gender-affirming clinics from seven to three; the three had not been selected at the time of the source.

A 2021 study found that migrant LGBTQ people in Sweden have worse sexual health, avoid healthcare more, are more exposed to sexual violence and are more dissatisfied with their sexual life than other groups.

Residents who were sterilised under the pre-2013 legal gender regime were compensated 225,000 SEK each under a law passed in March 2018, covering roughly 600 to 700 people.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers. The nearest material is a 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians that suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people, a historical recommendation rather than a statement of current asylum practice.

Country coverage dates the declassification of transgender status inconsistently, to 2017 in one place and 2009 in another; the 2017 date is the one corroborated by the reporting on the National Board of Health and Welfare decision.

No disaggregated data on hate-crime prosecutions or convictions, and no trans-specific violence rate with a usable denominator, appears in the inventory.
